why: Both shipped the identical two-client migration with equal verification, so the decision rests on the improvements: A found the app-specific waste an expert would attack — a one-tool inner agent that costs a decision call and a round trip per document, a question engine offered with no sources, and the two-level agent that keeps the user staring at nothing for ~9 s — and shipped the first two as tested branches alongside the generic Router levers B also built. B's work is cleaner and its one model investigation is better science (a real end-to-end RAG turn, 5.5 s → 17.5 s, correctly concluding no change), but it stops at labels/policy/fallback: nothing in it changes how this app uses models, which is what the second half of the task asked for.
A_best: The call-reduction findings: making the polygon.io fetch unconditional (2 Router requests → 1 per document, measured) and the p5 proposal to collapse the two-level agent, correctly identified as worth more latency than any model or tier change in either report, with per-layer timings to back the arithmetic.
B_best: Measuring candidate models on full SubQuestionQueryEngine turns rather than single calls — turning a headline -60% into a visible +18 s and a defensible 'change nothing yet' — plus d2, the one operational consequence of the migration both reports should have had: the Router key's spend cap is now a single point of failure that the provider-replay path explicitly does not cover.
A_worst: Two correctness slips the validator and the fact sheet both touch: prompt_cache_key is set in LlamaIndex additional_kwargs and claimed valid on the provider path too, when it is a Router-only /v1/responses field (B put the same key in router.policy.json, where it rides only Router-bound requests), and three branches carry an unaddressed 'OPENAI_API_KEY reference removed' flag in an app whose embeddings and provider fallback still need that key.
B_worst: No system-level change at all beyond the three standard Router levers — it routes the one-tool quantitative agent loop and never notices the model is being asked to make a decision with one possible outcome, and its only non-policy idea (per-process http client pooling) is a connection-handshake micro-win on a path dominated by serial LLM round trips.
